summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes CortexBridge, an adapter that maps arbitrary EEG electrode layouts into a shared cortical latent space using electrode and atlas coordinates. Unlike prior coordinate-driven methods that remain in scalp space, CortexBridge uses an anatomically grounded routing mechanism to interface with frozen foundation models. Evaluation on five MOABB datasets across three paradigms shows consistent performance gains for EEGPT, LaBraM, and CBraMod.

headline_results: Improved 13/15 evaluations across three foundation models.
Average gains: EEGPT (0.80%), LaBraM (0.70%), CBraMod (3.26%).
Maximum gain of 13.02% on SSVEP classification.

key_points: Method for EEG-FM adaptation: Proposes CortexBridge, a lightweight adapter that aligns arbitrary scalp montages to a shared cortical atlas space.
Anatomically grounded routing: Uses electrode coordinates and the Schaefer atlas to learn sparse ROI routing and multi-scale cortical interactions.
Broad empirical gains: Improves 13 of 15 evaluations across three frozen foundation models and three EEG paradigms, with a peak gain of 13.02% in SSVEP classification.
limitations: Evaluation limited to five public datasets and three EEG paradigms.
Needs extension to more recording systems and larger participant populations.
Lacks theoretical analysis of the learned cortical mapping.

method.architecture: Lightweight adapter using coordinate-aware cross-attention for sparse electrode-to-ROI routing (Schaefer atlas), multi-scale Gaussian diffusion for cortical interactions, and a residual interface.
method.finetuning: Trained as a lightweight interface to map raw EEG inputs to the latent space of frozen models (EEGPT, LaBraM, CBraMod).
method.objective: Task-specific loss combined with a column-balance penalty to ensure balanced ROI utilization.
method.pretraining: None; the adapter is trained on downstream tasks while the backbone foundation models remain frozen.

summary.one_liner: A lightweight adapter that aligns heterogeneous EEG montages to a shared cortical atlas space for better transfer to frozen foundation models.
summary.title: CortexBridge: Cortical Alignment of EEG Montages for Foundation Models
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces cortical alignment as a learnable, anatomically grounded routing mechanism to map heterogeneous EEG montages into a shared cortical latent space for foundation model adaptation.

papers.title: CortexBridge: Cortical Alignment of EEG Montages for Foundation Models

reasons: Explicitly targets EEG foundation models, specifically mentioning EEGPT, LaBraM, and CBraMod.
Proposes a cortical alignment adapter to solve montage heterogeneity for pretrained EEG-FMs.
Fits the EEG-FM ecosystem criteria as a work on adaptation and alignment for broad transfer.

summary.detailed_summary: ZeroMAG proposes a method to extend frozen EEG foundation models (EFMs) to multimodal recordings without requiring target labels or target-side optimization. It utilizes a configuration-invariant adapter architecture and a two-stage generator—combining a VAE-based representation learner and a conditional diffusion model—to produce adapter weights in a function-constrained latent space. Evaluation across six held-out datasets and three EFM backbones shows that ZeroMAG significantly outperforms EEG-only inference and approaches the performance of supervised multimodal adaptation.

headline_results: Improved balanced accuracy by 7.22% over EEG-only and 4.89% over direct weight regression
Within 0.50 percentage points of supervised multimodal adaptation

key_points: Method for zero-shot multimodal adaptation: Extends frozen EEG foundation models to include companion physiological signals without target-side training or labels.
Function-constrained generation: Employs a two-stage process using a VAE and a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) to ensure generated adapters maintain predictive consistency with reference adapters.
Strong empirical performance: Improves balanced accuracy by 7.22 percentage points over EEG-only baselines and nearly matches supervised multimodal adaptation across six held-out datasets.
limitations: Depends on the availability and quality of source reference adapters.
Requires a compatible prediction head trained on source data for the supported task.
Performance is dependent on the coverage and quality of the unlabeled calibration data.
Does not establish transferability of a single generator to arbitrary new architectures.

method.architecture: 1+N adapter (frozen EEG anchor + modality-specific branches) with a DiT-based generator.
method.objective: Function-preserving reconstruction and conditional latent diffusion.
method.pretraining: Two-stage training involving VAE representation learning followed by DiT conditional generation.

summary.one_liner: A zero-shot framework that generates multimodal adapters for frozen EEG foundation models using unlabeled target data and task context.
summary.title: ZeroMAG: Zero-Shot Multimodal Adapter Generation for Plug-and-Play EEG Foundation Models
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a zero-shot adapter generation pipeline that maps unlabeled target recordings and task context to functional adapter weights via a conditional diffusion model.

papers.title: ZeroMAG: Zero-Shot Multimodal Adapter Generation for Plug-and-Play EEG Foundation Models

reasons: Explicitly targets EEG foundation models (EFMs) and their reusable knowledge.
Proposes a framework (ZeroMAG) for adapting frozen EEG-FM encoders to multimodal recordings.
Evaluates the approach using three different EFM backbones.

summary.detailed_summary: SPERA proposes a latent-space prediction framework based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) to avoid reconstructing non-neural artifacts. It introduces a Legendre-polynomial spatial prior to encode scalp electrode geometry and a relational spectral regularizer to align latent similarities with spectral views. The model was pretrained on 80,000 hours of EEG from 106 datasets and demonstrated state-of-the-art average balanced accuracy across nine downstream clinical, cognitive, and BCI tasks.

headline_results: Achieved the highest average balanced accuracy across all 9 evaluated downstream tasks compared to other foundation models.

key_points: New EEG foundation model: SPERA utilizes a JEPA-style latent prediction objective to learn representations robust to non-neural artifacts.
Incorporates a learnable Legendre-polynomial spatial prior to handle heterogeneous electrode montages across different datasets.
Achieves superior performance across nine diverse downstream tasks using a massive pretraining corpus of 80,000 EEG hours.
limitations: High computational overhead for dense pairwise Legendre bias in full-attention blocks.
Dependence on 3D electrode coordinates or standard montage mappings.
Pretraining data distribution is heavily skewed toward clinical recordings (82.08%).

method.architecture: Hybrid Transformer backbone interleaving factorized (temporal/spatial) and full-attention blocks, using a Legendre-polynomial spherical prior.
method.finetuning: Linear Probing (LP) and Linear Probing followed by Fine-Tuning (LPFT).
method.objective: JEPA latent prediction objective combined with a Relational Spectral Regularizer (RSReg) based on KL divergence of similarity matrices.
method.pretraining: Large-scale pretraining on a multi-domain EEG corpus comprising 80,000 hours of data.

summary.one_liner: A JEPA-based EEG foundation model using a Legendre-polynomial spherical prior and relational spectral regularization to handle diverse electrode geometries and frequency components.
summary.title: SPERA: Spherical Prior EEG Foundation Model with Geometry- and Frequency-Aware Latent Prediction
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a Legendre-polynomial spherical prior and a relational spectral regularizer within a JEPA framework to create a geometry- and frequency-aware EEG foundation model.

papers.title: SPERA: Spherical Prior EEG Foundation Model with Geometry- and Frequency-Aware Latent Prediction

reasons: Explicitly identifies as an 'EEG foundation model' designed as a 'general-purpose backbone'.
Pretrained on a massive scale (80,000 hours of EEG from 106 datasets) for broad transfer.
Demonstrates utility across nine diverse downstream tasks spanning clinical, cognitive, and BCI applications.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes the Universal Semantic EEG Foundation Model (USE-FM), a parameter-efficient autoencoder pretrained on the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus (TUEG) via self-supervised signal reconstruction. Unlike larger existing models, USE-FM utilizes a frozen-encoder protocol for downstream tasks, demonstrating that a compact architecture with only 1.46 million parameters can learn transferable semantic representations. Evaluation on TUAB and TUEP datasets shows competitive performance compared to larger models like LUNA-Base and CBraMod, supported by latent space analysis using clustering and visualization.
key_points: New EEG foundation model: USE-FM is a lightweight CNN-Transformer autoencoder with only 1.46M parameters, approximately one-fifth the size of existing models.
Employs a frozen-encoder transfer protocol on TUAB and TUEP, achieving competitive results including an AUC of 85.24% on TUAB and an F1-score of 70.37% on TUEP.
Validates the organization of the learned latent space through k-means clustering, PCA, and t-SNE visualization, showing representations comparable to larger models.
limitations: Relies on a frozen-encoder protocol which may limit peak performance compared to full fine-tuning.
Evaluation is limited to two specific downstream datasets (TUAB and TUEP).
The architecture is adapted from a prior framework rather than being a completely novel design.
summary.one_liner: A lightweight CNN-Transformer EEG foundation model that achieves competitive cross-disorder transfer performance using a frozen-encoder protocol.
summary.title: Lightweight Semantic EEG Foundation Model for Frozen Cross-Disorder Transfer
summary.unique_contribution: Demonstrates that a lightweight EEG foundation model can learn universal semantic representations capable of competitive frozen-transfer across neurological disorders without requiring millions of parameters.

papers.title: Lightweight Semantic EEG Foundation Model for Frozen Cross-Disorder Transfer

reasons: Explicitly proposes the Universal Semantic EEG Foundation Model (USE-FM) for transferable neural representations.
Uses self-supervised pretraining on the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus (TUEG) for broad transfer.
Evaluates the model using a frozen-transfer protocol across multiple distinct downstream clinical tasks.
Directly compares the proposed model against existing EEG foundation models like LUNA-Base and CBraMod.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper introduces SpecBraM, which replaces traditional waveform reconstruction or discrete code prediction with the prediction of fixed narrow-band log spectral energy for masked patches. This approach avoids the irreducible noise of phase-sensitive waveform reconstruction and aligns the pretext task with the spectral features used in clinical EEG readouts. Evaluation on ISRUC and HMC sleep staging datasets shows that masked band-power prediction (MBP) significantly improves balanced accuracy and label efficiency compared to waveform-based targets.

headline_results: Balanced accuracy of 0.7916 (ISRUC) and 0.7425 (HMC) using frozen features
Outperforms CBraMod and LaBraM on 7 downstream tasks using frozen features

key_points: New EEG foundation model: SpecBraM utilizes masked band-power prediction instead of waveform reconstruction to learn more robust spectral representations.
Demonstrates superior label efficiency, with MBP exceeding waveform targets by 4.7-7.3 balanced-accuracy points when using only 1% of labels for sleep staging.
Shows that frozen features outperform existing models like CBraMod and LaBraM across seven downstream tasks, though gains are task-dependent.
limitations: Performance gains do not extend to all spectral-cue tasks, such as motor imagery and depression screening.
Vigilance regression results suggest potential low-frequency ocular contamination in the pretraining target.
The optimal frequency band partition and estimator remain unexplored.

method.finetuning: Linear probing and full fine-tuning on downstream tasks
method.objective: MSE of predicted vs actual log spectral energy in 5 narrow bands with SIGReg isotropy penalty
method.pretraining: Masked Band-Power Prediction (MBP) on TUEG dataset

summary.one_liner: SpecBraM proposes masked band-power prediction as a task-aligned pretraining target for EEG foundation models, outperforming waveform reconstruction in sleep staging.
summary.title: SpecBraM: What Should an EEG Foundation Model Predict? Masked Band-Power Prediction versus Waveform Reconstruction
summary.unique_contribution: Proposes masked band-power prediction (MBP) as a pretraining target to align EEG foundation models with the spectral physical quantities relevant to downstream clinical tasks.

papers.title: SpecBraM: What Should an EEG Foundation Model Predict? Masked Band-Power Prediction versus Waveform Reconstruction

reasons: Title explicitly mentions 'EEG Foundation Model'.
Focuses on comparing pretraining targets (masked band-power prediction vs waveform reconstruction) for reusable EEG representations.
Utilizes large-scale pretraining (2,388 hours) and evaluates via linear probing and fine-tuning across multiple downstream tasks.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper investigates how increasing the number of subjects affects cross-modal EEG-video alignment using the HBN dataset. It identifies a critical onset at approximately 50 subjects, below which scaling is unproductive, but above which decoding performance improves log-linearly. The authors show that initializing the encoder from a pretrained EEG foundation model (REVE) increases the scaling exponent by approximately 1.6x and reduces the compute required to reach convergence compared to random initialization.

headline_results: Log-linear scaling above 50 subjects
1.6x scaling acceleration with FM initialization
Superior top-1 retrieval accuracy for pretrained models

key_points: Method study on EEG scaling: reveals that naturalistic video decoding improves log-linearly with subject count only after a threshold of ~50 participants.
Foundation model advantage: initializing with REVE weights enables 1.6x faster scaling per cohort doubling and superior retrieval accuracy compared to random initialization.
Compute efficiency: pretrained encoders reach better performance optima using a fraction of the training compute (e.g., 26.6 vs 63.3 PFLOPs).
limitations: Results based on a single dataset (HBN) and montage.
Only one training stimulus and one transfer target used.
Small number of draws per cell limits p-value precision.
High subject overlap (86%) at the top rung of the scaling ladder.
Capacity axis limited to only two depths (12 and 22).
No comprehensive hyperparameter sweep performed for each arm.

method.finetuning: Cross-modal alignment with V-JEPA-2 vision teacher

summary.one_liner: Demonstrates a log-linear scaling law for EEG-video decoding that activates above 50 subjects and is significantly accelerated by EEG foundation model initialization.
summary.title: Scaling subjects in cross-modal alignment: video decoding with EEG foundation model
summary.unique_contribution: Identifies a subject-count onset (S ≈ 50) for productive scaling in EEG-video alignment and proves that EEG-FM initialization significantly accelerates this scaling.

papers.title: Scaling subjects in cross-modal alignment: video decoding with EEG foundation model

reasons: Explicitly focuses on scaling and initializing from an EEG foundation model
Investigates cross-modal alignment (EEG-video) as a frontier for EEG-FM scaling
Evaluates the performance gains of EEG-FM initialization over random initialization

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes BraVista, a framework that encodes multichannel EEG signals into structured STFT spectrogram images to interface with pretrained vision-language models (VLMs). Unlike prior EEG foundation models that require large-scale EEG-specific pretraining, BraVista leverages the visual and linguistic priors of a general-domain VLM through continued post-training. The approach is evaluated on four diverse datasets (sleep, emotion, workload, and abnormality detection), demonstrating that structured visual representations enable effective unified multi-task decoding.

headline_results: STFT images significantly outperformed raw time-series and topographies
Achieved strong balanced accuracy across four diverse EEG decoding tasks

key_points: New EEG foundation model: BraVista utilizes a vision-language model (Qwen3-VL-2B) to decode EEG signals by treating them as structured images.
Method novelty: Employs STFT-based image grids and instruction-conditioning to enable multi-task learning across diverse BCI applications.
Evidence: Outperforms zero-shot VLMs and shows robustness to noise across sleep staging, emotion recognition, cognitive workload, and abnormality detection tasks.
limitations: Focuses on producing class labels without explicitly leveraging the reasoning capabilities of VLMs.
Lacks integration of subject-specific metadata or clinical history.
Does not employ reinforcement learning to guide model reasoning across temporal segments.

method.architecture: Qwen3-VL-2B (SigLIP-2 vision encoder, vision-language merger, and language model decoder)
method.finetuning: Full fine-tuning of the vision encoder and LoRA for the language model decoder
method.objective: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for autoregressive conditional generation
method.pretraining: Leverages general-domain VLM priors from Qwen3-VL

summary.one_liner: BraVista adapts general-domain vision-language models to EEG decoding by representing multichannel signals as structured STFT images.
summary.title: Multimodal LLMs Can Learn to Read Brain Signals: A Vision--Language Model for Unified Multi-Task EEG Decoding
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a structured visual interface using STFT spectrogram grids that allows general-domain VLMs to perform unified multi-task EEG decoding without EEG-specific pretraining.

papers.title: Multimodal LLMs Can Learn to Read Brain Signals: A Vision--Language Model for Unified Multi-Task EEG Decoding

reasons: Focuses on unified multi-task EEG decoding across diverse datasets (sleep, emotion, workload, abnormal EEG).
Proposes a framework to adapt general-domain foundation models (VLMs) to EEG signals via continued post-training.
Explicitly aims to learn EEG representations that generalize across cognitive tasks, subjects, and recording conditions.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes DEFT, a post-backbone adapter designed to mitigate the burden of subject-related variation in pretrained EEG foundation model (EFM) embeddings. It factorizes mixed pretrained tokens into a task-content branch and a subject-style branch using a recursive Gaussian disentangler, guided by temporal-variance regularization, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction. Experiments across four EFM backbones and six diverse EEG datasets demonstrate that performing downstream prediction solely from the isolated content branch consistently improves performance over vanilla fine-tuning in cross-subject settings.

headline_results: Consistent improvement in Balanced Accuracy (B-ACC) over vanilla fine-tuning across four EFM backbones.

key_points: Method for EFM fine-tuning: Proposes DEFT, a plug-and-play adapter that separates pretrained tokens into content and style branches to reduce subject-related bias.
Novel disentanglement mechanism: Uses recursive Gaussian refinement and temporal-variance constraints to ensure content captures dynamics while style captures stable subject traits.
Broad empirical validation: Improves performance across four foundation backbones and six diverse EEG tasks, particularly in cross-subject scenarios.
limitations: Requires subject identity labels during training for the contrastive loss.
Performance gains vary across different datasets and backbones.
The method is a post-backbone adapter and does not modify the pretraining phase.

method.architecture: Post-backbone adapter with Recursive Gaussian Disentangler and dual branches (Content/Style).
method.finetuning: Disentanglement-enhanced fine-tuning where the classifier operates only on the content branch.
method.objective: Combined loss including cross-entropy, temporal-variance, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction.

summary.one_liner: A plug-and-play adapter for EEG foundation models that disentangles task-oriented content from subject-specific style to improve cross-subject decoding.
summary.title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a 'factorize-before-classify' adapter that explicitly separates subject-consistent style from task-oriented content in pretrained EEG representations to reduce classifier burden.

papers.title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models

reasons: Explicitly targets EEG foundation models (EFMs) in both title and abstract.
Proposes a specific fine-tuning method (DEFT) designed for EFM backbones.
Focuses on improving the utility of pretrained EEG representations for downstream tasks.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes a task-semantic alignment framework that maps EEG signals from a single anterior-posterior differential channel into a shared semantic space with task descriptions. Unlike task-agnostic self-supervised learning, this approach uses a sentence encoder to embed experimental instructions, stimuli, and response demands, allowing the model to rank candidate tasks without target-specific calibration. Evaluation on a ten-class task demonstrates zero-shot balanced accuracy of 30.13% and few-shot accuracy reaching 74.99% when using the test participant's own recordings.

headline_results: Zero-shot: 30.13% balanced accuracy
Few-shot (cross-participant): 34.47%
Few-shot (within-participant): 74.99%

key_points: New EEG foundation model: Aligns single-channel EEG signals with semantic embeddings of task instructions and stimuli for cognitive state decoding.
Achieves zero-shot task prediction with 30.13% balanced accuracy (vs 10% chance) and significant few-shot gains up to 74.99%.
Identifies that training on datasets with multiple tasks per participant is more effective for transfer than adding datasets with limited task variety.
limitations: Zero-shot performance remains relatively low compared to within-participant few-shot performance.
Adding datasets with only one or a few tasks per participant can sometimes reduce performance.
The model is constrained to a single anterior-posterior differential channel.

method.architecture: EEG encoder aligned with a sentence encoder's task vectors
method.finetuning: Few-shot adaptation using small sets of target task examples
method.objective: Contrastive-style alignment of EEG signals with semantic task embeddings
method.pretraining: Trained on publicly available EEG data from various labs

summary.one_liner: A framework that aligns single-channel EEG signals with semantic task embeddings to enable zero-shot and few-shot cognitive task prediction.
summary.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a method to align single-channel EEG signals with structured task-semantic vectors to facilitate zero-shot transfer across diverse cognitive tasks.

papers.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment

reasons: EEG is the central modality used for predicting cognitive tasks.
The paper proposes a task-semantic alignment framework to enable zero-shot and few-shot transfer.
The abstract explicitly frames the findings as being useful for training an EEG foundation model.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper investigates how unsupervised autoencoders (LSTMVAE, VAEEG, Transformer) and the REVE foundation model handle the characteristic 1/f power decay of EEG signals. It demonstrates that Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss leads to a magnitude-driven masking effect, where high-frequency information is under-represented in the latent space. Using synthetic data and the BBHI empirical dataset, the authors show that while low-frequency shifts like alpha slowing are captured, high-frequency transients are often lost unless latent dimensionality is significantly increased.

headline_results: Confirmed magnitude-driven masking of high-frequency components in MSE-based autoencoders.
Demonstrated that latent dimensionality must be significantly increased to capture high-frequency transients.

key_points: Methodological analysis of EEG representation learning: examines spectral biases across various autoencoder architectures and the REVE foundation model.
Reveals that standard time-domain reconstruction losses prioritize high-power low frequencies, effectively smoothing out high-frequency transients.
Demonstrates that increasing latent dimensionality can mitigate spectral attenuation but compromises model compactness and generative stability.
limitations: Synthetic data simplifies non-linear dynamics and omits inter-channel correlations.
Empirical validation on BBHI used only a single seed due to compute constraints.
Increasing latent dimensionality to fix spectral bias reduces generative stability.
The study focuses primarily on unsupervised reconstruction rather than supervised downstream tasks.

method.architecture: Evaluation of LSTMVAE, VAEEG, and Transformer autoencoders, alongside the frozen REVE foundation model (Transformer encoder).
method.objective: Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) for reconstruction; masked-autoencoding for REVE.
method.pretraining: REVE was pretrained on 60,000 hours of EEG data.

summary.one_liner: Systematic analysis of spectral bias in unsupervised EEG representation learning, revealing that time-domain reconstruction losses mask critical high-frequency biomarkers.
summary.title: Spectral Considerations on Unsupervised Time-domain EEG Representation Learning with Deep Networks
summary.unique_contribution: Identifies a magnitude-driven masking effect in time-domain EEG autoencoders that suppresses high-frequency biomarkers due to the interaction between MSE loss and the 1/f power spectrum.

papers.title: Spectral Considerations on Unsupervised Time-domain EEG Representation Learning with Deep Networks

reasons: EEG is the primary modality.
Explicitly evaluates a state-of-the-art EEG foundation model.
Provides systematic analysis of unsupervised representations to improve future large-scale foundation-level feature extractors.

summary.detailed_summary: HyBRA proposes a hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation mechanism to handle heterogeneous electrode montages by mapping channel tokens to a fixed regional space. It combines electrode coordinates and region priors with feature-dependent hyperbolic distances and a channel-evidence injection branch to preserve fine-grained cues. The model is pretrained via masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals, demonstrating superior balanced accuracy across six benchmark datasets compared to existing foundation models.

headline_results: Macro-averaged balanced accuracy of 0.7278 across six benchmarks.
96.8% fewer parameters than CSBrain on OpenBMI-MI.

key_points: New EEG foundation model: HyBRA uses hyperbolic global-local aggregation to create a montage-independent regional representation.
Employs a Region-Time Transformer pretrained with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals.
Outperforms existing models on six benchmarks, achieving higher balanced accuracy with significantly fewer parameters.
limitations: Performance gains on some datasets like TUAB and Siena are smaller than on others.
Does not uniformly improve every secondary metric, such as AUROC on specific datasets.
Relies on predefined brain-region priors for channel-region associations.

method.architecture: Coordinate-Aware Patch Encoding, Hyperbolic Region Mixer, and Region-Time Transformer.
method.finetuning: End-to-end fine-tuning with a compact CNN head for downstream tasks.
method.objective: Masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals.
method.pretraining: Self-supervised pretraining on seven datasets using masked reconstruction.

summary.one_liner: A self-supervised EEG framework that maps heterogeneous channel observations into a fixed regional token space using hyperbolic geometry.
summary.title: HyBRA-EEG: Hyperbolic Global-Local Brain-Region Aggregation for Self-Supervised EEG Representation Learning
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a hyperbolic region mixer and a channel-evidence injection pathway to map heterogeneous EEG montages into a consistent, fixed regional token space.

papers.title: HyBRA-EEG: Hyperbolic Global-Local Brain-Region Aggregation for Self-Supervised EEG Representation Learning

reasons: Focuses on self-supervised EEG pretraining to improve transferability across heterogeneous recordings
Uses a masked reconstruction objective for pretraining, a core characteristic of foundation models
Evaluates the resulting representations across six benchmark datasets

summary.detailed_summary: The paper evaluates the utility of frozen representations from prominent self-supervised PSG foundation models (SleepFM, OSF, Hypnos) and large-scale supervised encoders (U-Sleep, SleepTransformer) for multilabel identification of six sleep-wake and circadian disorder groups. Using a common Coupled Mamba downstream framework on 7,906 PSGs, the authors find that supervised encoders pretrained at comparable scale and modality coverage match or exceed the performance of self-supervised FMs. The results highlight that respiratory modality coverage and pretraining scale are more critical for clinical disorder identification than the choice of self-supervised versus supervised objectives.

headline_results: Supervised encoders matched or outperformed self-supervised FMs when scale and modality coverage were comparable.
tasks: Multilabel identification of 6 sleep-wake and circadian disorder groups

key_points: Benchmark study: Compares self-supervised PSG foundation models against large-scale supervised encoders for identifying six sleep-wake and circadian disorder groups.
Findings show that supervised pretraining at comparable scale and modality coverage (especially respiratory signals) matches or exceeds self-supervised performance.
Supervised encoders exhibited superior downstream data efficiency compared to self-supervised foundation models.
limitations: Evaluated on a single tertiary referral registry, which may limit generalizability.
SWCD identification is closely related to sleep architecture, potentially favoring staging-based representations.
Did not perform fully factorial retraining across all architectures and corpora due to scale.

method.architecture: Frozen representations from U-Sleep, SleepTransformer, SleepFM, OSF, and Hypnos fed into a mask-aware Coupled Mamba state-space model.
method.finetuning: Linear probing/downstream training of the Coupled Mamba head.
method.objective: Multilabel classification of six disorder groups.
method.pretraining: Supervised sleep-staging (U-Sleep, SleepTransformer) and various self-supervised objectives (SleepFM, OSF, Hypnos).

summary.one_liner: A large-scale benchmark comparing self-supervised PSG foundation models against large-scale supervised sleep-staging encoders for sleep-wake disorder identification.
summary.title: On Sleep-Wake Disorder Identification from Polysomnographic Representations
summary.unique_contribution: Demonstrates that large-scale, multi-cohort supervised sleep-staging encoders can outperform self-supervised PSG foundation models in identifying clinical sleep-wake disorders when modality coverage is matched.

papers.title: On Sleep-Wake Disorder Identification from Polysomnographic Representations

reasons: Explicitly evaluates 'Self-supervised polysomnography foundation models (PSG FMs)' and their downstream potential.
Uses frozen representations from large-scale pretrained models for transfer learning tasks.
PSG is a multimodal signal where EEG is a central and core modality.
Fits the ecosystem criteria as a benchmark/evaluation of foundation model representations against supervised baselines.

summary.detailed_summary: NeuroAct proposes a dual-loop autonomous research agent framework designed to improve EEG decoding by explicitly diagnosing signal structure, representations, and training dynamics. Unlike prior reward-driven search methods, it employs an inner loop for hypothesis testing and an outer loop to distill and reuse conditional recommendations across different tasks. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated across four research settings using six datasets, showing significant gains in balanced accuracy and efficiency through experience reuse.

headline_results: Setting A: 80.88 macro-average
Setting B: EEGPT BA +7.34 points
Setting C: ADFTD BA +16.33 points
Setting D: Workload BA 85.02%

key_points: New research method: An autonomous agent framework that employs a dual-loop system to guide EEG analysis and decoding through evidence-based diagnostics.
Implements an inner loop for hypothesis-driven model refinement and an outer loop for distilling conditional recommendations that improve performance on subsequent tasks.
Demonstrated significant improvements across multiple benchmarks, including a 16.33 point BA gain on ADFTD and a 16.15 point BA increase on BCIC-IV-2a via experience reuse.
limitations: High reliance on LLM token budgets (capped at 50M tokens per study).
Performance is dependent on the quality of the LLM backend used.
Requires access to a pool of existing EEG foundation models for collaborative prediction.
Computational cost of running multiple iterative experiments in the inner loop.

method.architecture: Dual-loop agent framework (Coordinator, Researcher, Developer, Reviewer) utilizing LLM backends (DeepSeek-V4 Flash, GPT-5.6 Luna, Qwen3.8 Flash Next).
method.finetuning: Task-specific adaptation, model combination, and joint multi-task training guided by the agent.
method.objective: Optimize EEG decoding performance (BA, AUROC, Pearson r) and research efficiency (token cost).
method.pretraining: N/A (uses existing EEG-FMs like EEGPT, BENDR, LaBraM).

summary.one_liner: An autonomous research agent framework that uses a dual-loop system to optimize EEG analysis and decoding through evidence-guided diagnostics and cross-task experience reuse.
summary.title: NeuroAct: Advancing EEG Analysis and Decoding via Dual-Loop Autonomous Research
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a dual-loop autonomous agent that leverages explicit diagnostic evidence and cross-task experience reuse to optimize EEG foundation model adaptation and decoding.

papers.title: NeuroAct: Advancing EEG Analysis and Decoding via Dual-Loop Autonomous Research

reasons: Explicitly mentions implementing autonomous research across 'EEG foundation models'.
Demonstrates performance improvements on EEGPT, a known EEG foundation model.
Targets the EEG-FM ecosystem through cross-task model optimization and adaptation.

summary.detailed_summary: BrainCodes proposes a compact foundation model combining a frozen RVQ tokenizer with a factorized Transformer U-Net backbone. Unlike typical reconstruction-based models, it employs masked discrete code prediction and an auxiliary task of detecting synthetic narrowband bursts to preserve physiologically relevant features. Evaluation across 14 benchmarks, including consumer-grade wearables, shows it matches or exceeds larger SOTA models while using significantly fewer parameters.

headline_results: Achieved highest mean nBAC among compared foundation models
Maintained high performance on sparse consumer-grade montages

key_points: New EEG foundation model: BrainCodes uses a quantization-based tokenizer and a factorized Transformer U-Net to learn transferable features with only 1.9M parameters.
Novel pretraining: Combines masked discrete code prediction with an auxiliary objective that injects synthetic narrowband bursts to ensure sensitivity to neural oscillations.
Strong transferability: Outperforms baselines on low-resource wearable devices and retains 91% of full-montage performance with only 4 electrodes.
limitations: Pretraining corpus consists primarily of children and adolescents, potentially limiting generalization to older adults.
The model relies on a frozen external tokenizer, making the total system footprint dependent on that component.
Evaluation on consumer-grade hardware is limited to a small number of datasets.

method.architecture: Frozen RVQ tokenizer (BioCodec) + Factorized Transformer U-Net with 3D rotary positional encoding for channels.
method.finetuning: Linear probing and full fine-tuning of the backbone for downstream tasks.
method.objective: Masked discrete code prediction (primary) and region oscillation injection (auxiliary).

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes a set of spatial and spectral perturbation probes to assess if EEG foundation models (EEG-FMs) are grounded in physiological properties like electrode locality and waveform morphology. By testing five existing EEG-FMs (BIOT, LaBraM, CBraMod, CSBrain, REVE) on motor-imagery and seizure datasets, the authors demonstrate a dissociation between what a model encodes in its representations and what it actually uses for downstream predictions. Results show that while some models are sensitive to spatial or spectral perturbations in their latent space, this sensitivity does not always translate to changes in classification accuracy.

headline_results: REVE showed the strongest spatial and spectral grounding.
Observed dissociation between representational sensitivity and downstream reliance across most models.

key_points: Benchmark study: evaluates five EEG foundation models using perturbation probes to test spatial and spectral grounding.
Reveals a dissociation where representational sensitivity to signal properties does not necessarily imply downstream reliance for task accuracy.
Finds that REVE exhibits the strongest grounding in both topographic locality and clinical waveform morphology compared to other tested models.
limitations: Evaluation is limited to five specific published EEG foundation models.
Probing is performed using only linear readouts on frozen encoders.
The dataset size for probing is a subset of the full available data.
Clinical markers used in spectral probes are synthetic/simulated.

method.architecture: Perturbation-based probing framework applied to frozen EEG-FM encoders with linear readouts.
method.objective: Evaluation of representational sensitivity via latent displacement and downstream accuracy drop.

summary.one_liner: Introduces a perturbation-based probing framework to evaluate whether EEG foundation models encode and rely on physiologically interpretable spatial and spectral signal structures.
summary.title: Probing Spatial and Spectral Grounding in EEG Foundation Models
summary.unique_contribution: A systematic probing framework that disentangles architectural access, representational encoding, and functional reliance on spatial and spectral grounding in EEG foundation models.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes a controlled evaluation protocol for EEG foundation models incorporating random initialization, band-power baselines, and validation-selected probes. It evaluates six models (five public and one in-house) across nine benchmarks, finding that many reported gains vanish when layers are selected on validation rather than test sets. The results demonstrate that random initialization often matches pretraining on specific tasks and that simple band-power features frequently outperform complex foundation models on emotion and motor imagery.

headline_results: Test-selection inflates layer-wise peaks by +0.034 on average.
Band-power baselines are rarely beaten on emotion or motor imagery tasks.
Only 5 of 30 fine-tuning pairs showed gains beyond seed noise.

key_points: Benchmark study: Evaluates six EEG foundation models using a controlled protocol to identify overestimations in reported downstream gains.
Reveals that picking probed layers based on test scores inflates performance and that band-power baselines are rarely beaten on emotion or motor imagery tasks.
Finds that for many model-dataset pairs, random initialization performs comparably to pretraining under frozen probing.
limitations: The in-house model's SincNet filters acted as low-pass filters, limiting its ability to capture mu and beta rhythms for motor imagery.
Fine-tuning gains were measured using a shared canonical schedule, which serves as a lower bound rather than the absolute best per-model performance.
The number of seeds (5) is small, making it difficult to reach conventional statistical significance for every single cell.
Input handling differences across models are confounded with corpus and implementation maturity.

method.architecture: Evaluates five public models (LaBraM, EEGPT, CBraMod, LUNA, LuMamba) and one in-house JEPA-style model with a SincNet front-end and 8-layer transformer encoder.
method.finetuning: Comparison between frozen linear probing (validation-selected) and full fine-tuning using a shared canonical schedule.
method.objective: Comparison of pretraining objectives against random initialization and 5-band log-power baselines.
method.pretraining: The in-house model was pretrained on the REVE corpus using a JEPA-style objective with a SIGReg regularizer.

summary.one_liner: A systematic re-evaluation of EEG foundation models using rigorous controls to assess the actual gains of pretraining over random initialization and simple spectral baselines.

summary.detailed_summary: NOMAD-EEG introduces a generative diffusion-based architecture designed to be independent of electrode count, identity, order, and input length. It factorizes spatio-temporal mixing by alternating bidirectional S4D (State-Space Model) layers for patch-free temporal processing at 20ms resolution and multi-head attention for spatial mixing, where electrodes are identified via Fourier features of 3D scalp positions. Pre-trained on 147 hours of unlabelled TUEV data, the 12M-parameter model outperformed seven larger foundation models on various downstream tasks, including seizure detection and motor imagery, using frozen linear probes.

headline_results: Outperformed 7 other foundation models on several tasks
EEGMMIDB motor imagery: 0.442 balanced accuracy
Siena seizure detection: 0.622 macro F1
Bonn seizure detection: 0.999 AUROC

key_points: New EEG foundation model: A 12M-parameter diffusion model that is natively agnostic to electrode montage and input length.
Combines bidirectional S4D layers for patch-free temporal processing with 3D coordinate-conditioned attention for spatial mixing.
Outperformed seven larger foundation models on seizure detection and motor imagery benchmarks using frozen linear probes.
limitations: Pre-trained on a single EEG corpus (TUEV), which may limit generalizability compared to multi-corpus pre-training.
Scaling studies indicated that significantly larger models with more data did not yield substantial performance gains.
Performance depends on the availability and accuracy of 3D scalp coordinate metadata for electrodes.

method.architecture: Diffusion model with a convolutional stem and 16 blocks of alternating bidirectional S4D layers (temporal) and multi-head attention layers (spatial) using 3D scalp coordinates.
method.finetuning: Evaluated using frozen linear probes or token-based fine-tuning on downstream tasks.
method.objective: Denoising diffusion with a cosine noise schedule.
method.pretraining: Pre-trained on 147 hours of unlabelled EEG data from the TUEV corpus.

summary.one_liner: A montage- and length-agnostic generative EEG foundation model using diffusion, state-space layers, and 3D coordinate-based attention.
summary.title: NOMAD-EEG: Native Omni-Montage Adaptive Diffusion
summary.unique_contribution: The first EEG foundation model to simultaneously combine a generative diffusion objective, 3D position-based montage independence, and patch-free temporal modeling.
